title: The omelette
hookLine: can ordinary work be prayer? Lawrence turns an omelette for the love of God, and a neighbor tradition offers every act too
tomorrow: do you need a holier job to become holy?

cards: Cooking videos make it look like art: slow-motion butter, a perfect flip, a chef who never burns anything. Real kitchens are different. Dishes stacking up, a timer going off, someone asking when dinner's ready.
Brother Lawrence worked in his monastery's kitchen. And when he picked an example of a life with God, he didn't choose a vigil or a pilgrimage. He chose about the smallest job at the stove.
Which raises an old question: can ordinary work be prayer?

teach.b: Lawrence's answer, from the fourth conversation: we can do little things for God. He turns his little omelette in the pan for the love of God.
When it's done, if nothing else is calling him, he bows down in worship before the God who gave him the grace to work, and gets up, he says, happier than a king.

It's enough for him, he adds, to pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God. Notice what he never says: that the omelette turns holy because it's cooked perfectly. The size of the act stops mattering.
What changes it is who it's for. A neighbor tradition says something close.
In the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, Krishna, speaking as the Lord, tells the warrior Arjuna: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me.

What they share: everyday acts, even eating, can be offered to God. The honest difference: in the Gita, the offering belongs to a teaching about acting without clinging to the results, spoken on a battlefield.
Lawrence offers his work to the God he knows in Jesus, and he talks about it as a friendship, a conversation that goes on all day at the stove.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: a line about holiness that readers keep coming back to is about turning an omelette.

how: Many Catholics offer their daily work to God, some with a short morning offering; readers of Brother Lawrence often keep his kitchen in mind while cooking or cleaning.

o: a small kitchen job Lawrence did for the love of God
the only meal monks could eat on fast days
a dish Lawrence once cooked for a king's visit

p: turned for the love of God
worship, then up happier than a king

s: Lawrence thought work only counts for God if it's done perfectly
he never rates the cooking; what changes the act is who it's for.
after the omelette, Lawrence says he got up happier than a king
he bowed in worship, then rose, by his own account, happier than a king.
the Bhagavad Gita and Lawrence teach exactly the same thing
they share the offering of everyday acts; their frames and reasons differ.

games.q: your roommate cooks dinner every night and says it doesn't count as anything spiritual, it's just cooking. what would Lawrence say?
o: it can count: done for the love of God, even an omelette is enough.
it counts only if she prays out loud the whole time she cooks.
it counts if the food is excellent, because God deserves the best.
games.why: Lawrence never rates the cooking. picking up a straw for the love of God is enough, he says; what changes the act is who it's for.

practice: Hold something to taste: a mug of tea, a glass of water, a piece of bread or fruit. Smell it, then take one slow sip or bite, and offer it in your own words, to God or to someone you love.
Let the sit run with the taste still there.

wordCard.voice: The omelette. The smallest job at the stove, turned for the love of God, by a cook who got up happier than a king.

orig.note: Latin for 'for the love of God,' the Church's old words for Lawrence's reason.

carryVoice: The line for today: for love of god, even an omelette, even a straw picked up from the floor. Eat well tonight.
